Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrc}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
\midrule
All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
\label{tab:downstream}
\end{table}

The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.

Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.

\paragraph{Equivalence testing.}
We apply a two one-sided $t$-test (TOST) with a $\pm$2\% relative margin (equivalence bounds $\pm$0.047 on the ppl scale) to formally assess whether the depth-aware and random subsampling conditions produce practically indistinguishable perplexity.
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951): size-matched (random) ppl\,=\,2.367 vs.\ depth 0--1 ppl\,=\,2.387, $\Delta$\,=\,0.020.
TOST confirms equivalence ($p = 1.1 \times 10^{-4}$), indicating the two curation strategies yield practically indistinguishable downstream quality within the $\pm$2\% margin.
Cross-seed standard deviation is below 0.001 for both variants.

Comparing the full dataset ($n$\,=\,12{,}299, ppl\,=\,2.335) against the depth-filtered subset ($n$\,=\,3{,}951, ppl\,=\,2.387): TOST \emph{rejects} equivalence (minimum equivalence margin\,=\,0.053, exceeding the $\pm$2\% bound), confirming that data quantity drives perplexity reduction beyond what depth-aware selection can recover.

Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training; at fixed sample count, depth-aware curation is statistically equivalent to uninformed random subsampling.

\subsection*{Margin Sensitivity Analysis}

To assess the robustness of the equivalence conclusion to margin choice, we repeat the TOST procedure across multiple equivalence margins \cite{lakens_equivalence}, following the recommendation to report sensitivity across plausible bounds rather than relying on a single threshold (Table~\ref{tab:tost-margins}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Comparison} & \textbf{Margin} & \textbf{Equiv?} & \textbf{TOST $p$} \\
\midrule
Full (12{,}299) vs.\ Random (3{,}951) & $\pm$1\% & No & 1.0 \\
                                        & $\pm$2\% & Yes & $1 \times 10^{-6}$ \\
                                        & $\pm$3\% & Yes & $< 10^{-10}$ \\
                                        & $\pm$5\% & Yes & $< 10^{-10}$ \\
\midrule
Full (12{,}299) vs.\ Depth 0--1 (3{,}951) & $\pm$1\% & No & 1.0 \\
                                            & $\pm$2\% & No & 1.0 \\
                                            & $\pm$3\% & Yes & $< 10^{-10}$ \\
                                            & $\pm$5\% & Yes & $< 10^{-10}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\caption{TOST equivalence testing across multiple margins. ``Equiv?'' indicates whether equivalence is established at $\alpha = 0.05$.}
\label{tab:tost-margins}
\end{table}

The full dataset vs.\ random subsample comparison passes equivalence at the $\pm$2\% margin ($p = 10^{-6}$), while the full vs.\ depth 0--1 comparison requires a $\pm$3\% margin.
In absolute terms, perplexity differences are small: $\Delta$\,=\,0.032 (full vs.\ random, 1.4\% of baseline) and $\Delta$\,=\,0.052 (full vs.\ depth 0--1, 2.2\% of baseline).

Cohen's $d$ values are 86.0 (full vs.\ random) and 119.7 (full vs.\ depth 0--1).
These appear large but are unreliable: with only $n$\,=\,3 seeds per condition, the pooled standard deviation is extremely small ($<$0.001), artificially inflating $d$.
The inflated effect sizes reflect low seed-level variance (confirming reproducibility) rather than practically meaningful perplexity differences.
The TOST framework with pre-specified relative margins provides a more appropriate assessment than Cohen's $d$ in this low-seed regime.

2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Why does shape remain approximately stationary?}
5	The softmax architecture and sampling hyperparameters that determine distributional shape are fixed across depths; recursive generation shifts context toward high-probability regions but does not alter the generation mechanism itself.
6	This predicts approximate stationarity under standard decoding, confirmed by sampling ablation ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$: ${\leq}0.3$\,pp degradation; $t = 1.0$: $-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and implies the phenomenon reflects a tendency of standard decoding rather than an architectural guarantee.
7	Entropy std ($|\rho| = 0.17$) is a borderline case between the drifting central-tendency features ($|\rho| > 0.60$) and the near-stationary tail decay ($|\rho| = 0.04$), consistent with a feature that partially captures location-dependent variance.
8	
9	\paragraph{Prompt-type dependence.}
10	Semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}), consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}: the more a task anchors the output distribution to the input, the less room recursive drift has to accumulate.
11	Cross-type transfer remains viable (F1\,=\,0.753).
12	
13	\paragraph{Practical applicability.}
14	Document-level gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging, where error scales as $O(1/\sqrt{n})$.
15	Misclassifications concentrate in shallow gen-2+ samples where drift has not yet accumulated (Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}), consistent with DDR predictions.
16	
17	\paragraph{The gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ boundary.}
18	The primary classification difficulty is distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+: 86\% of binary errors are false negatives (gen-2+ predicted as gen-1), with depth-2 error rate at 48\% compared to 20\% for depth-4.
19	This asymmetry follows directly from DDR: the first recursive step produces the smallest location shift, so depth-2 text occupies a region of feature space that overlaps heavily with gen-1.
20	Larger generators exacerbate the overlap (Mistral-7B error rate 45\% vs.\ Pythia-1B 18\%), consistent with higher-capacity models producing text that more closely matches the statistical properties of human-sourced input.
21	
22	\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
23	Model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} describes degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs, progressively losing distributional coverage through parameter updates.
24	DDR operates in a fundamentally different regime: inference-chain drift occurs with fixed parameters, and is fully reversible by changing the seed text.
25	The two phenomena also diverge in their distributional signatures: model collapse predicts progressive tail shrinkage as minority modes are lost from the training distribution \cite{curse_of_recursion}, whereas DDR preserves distributional shape (entropy max, tail decay remain stationary) while shifting only the location.
26	This suggests that inference-chain drift reflects compression \emph{within} the model's existing capacity rather than \emph{erosion} of that capacity, and may represent a pre-collapse regime where distributional narrowing is detectable but not yet irreversible.
27	Topic drift shows weak correlation with depth features ($|\rho| < 0.29$; embedding similarity between successive generations correlates with entropy drift at $\rho = -0.286$), confirming it mediates rather than confounds depth signal.

1	\section*{Limitations}
2	\label{sec:limitations}
3	
4	All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
5	This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, enabling controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
6	However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
7	Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 under a 7-generator split).
8	Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
9	Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.
10	
11	Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
12	Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
13	Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, enabling controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 under a 7-generator split).
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show strongest drift (within-type F1\,=\,0.781) compared to elaboration (0.730), rewriting (0.737), and paraphrastic chains (binary F1\,=\,0.671 vs.\ 0.749 for continuation).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), though the eight generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under LOGO at $t{=}1.0$), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: certain domain/generator combinations at lower temperature approach chance level (e.g., Academic domain binary F1\,=\,0.628 at $t{=}0.7$), suggesting that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
The reference model dependency (Pythia-410M, English-centric pretraining) limits non-English applicability and adds inference overhead relative to surface-feature-only approaches.
Generalization to other languages remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A sampling ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows robustness to moderate variation ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$, ${\leq}0.3$\,pp) but substantial degradation at $t{=}1.0$ ($-6$\,pp), indicating that depth fingerprinting assumes standard decoding regimes.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\begin{figure*}[t]
5	\centering
6	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig2_framework.pdf}
7	\caption{Overview of the depth fingerprinting framework. Given a text, reference-model features (entropy statistics under Pythia-410M) and surface features (lexical diversity) are extracted and fed to an XGBoost classifier trained under Leave-One-Generator-Out cross-validation. The feature set combines drifting indicators (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio) that capture the monotonic location shift with stationary indicators (entropy max, tail decay) that provide a stable baseline, exploiting their differential depth response for ordinal classification.}
8	\label{fig:framework}
9	\end{figure*}
10	
11	\subsection{Task Formulation}
12	\label{sec:task}
13	
14	Given a text $x$, the goal is to predict its \emph{generation depth} $d \in \{0, 1, 2{+}\}$, where $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text, $d{=}1$ denotes first-generation LLM output conditioned on human text, and $d{=}2{+}$ denotes text produced by recursively conditioning an LLM on its own prior output at least twice.
15	Formally, let $\mathcal{C}_0$ be a reference corpus of human-written text.
16	A generation chain of depth $k$ is defined recursively: $x^{(0)} \sim \mathcal{C}_0$, and $x^{(k)} = G(x^{(k-1)})$ for $k \geq 1$, where $G$ denotes stochastic LLM generation conditioned on its input.
17	We frame depth estimation as an ordinal classification task over three classes rather than binary real-vs-synthetic detection, enabling finer-grained provenance characterization.
18	Depths beyond 2 are merged into a single $2{+}$ class, consistent with monotonic feature convergence that compresses inter-class margins beyond depth 2 (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
19	
20	\subsection{Generation Chain Construction}
21	\label{sec:generation}
22	
23	We construct generation chains using eight generators spanning five model families: \textbf{Pythia} (2.8B, 1B) \cite{pythia}, \textbf{OLMo} (OLMo-2-1B) \cite{olmo}, \textbf{Qwen} (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B-Base) \cite{qwen3}, \textbf{Llama} (Llama-3.2-3B) \cite{llama3}, and \textbf{Mistral} (Mistral-7B-v0.3) \cite{mistral7b}.
24	This selection covers parameter scales from 0.6B to 8B and diverse pretraining corpora, enabling evaluation of cross-generator and cross-scale generalization.
25	
26	For each generator, we sample approximately 1{,}000 seed passages from English Wikipedia as $\mathcal{C}_0$.
27	The same pool of seed passages serves as gen-0 for all generators.
28	We use shared seeds across generators to ensure that cross-generator comparisons control for input content, isolating the effect of the generation model from source text variation.
29	In LOGO evaluation, gen-0 samples from the held-out generator's chains also appear (with the same text) in the training generators' chains, creating a potential train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
30	We address this with a supplementary binary evaluation excluding gen-0 entirely (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
31	Each seed is iteratively fed through the generator to produce a chain of depth 4 (i.e., gen-0 through gen-4), using the prompt ``\texttt{Continue the following text: \{text\}}''.
32	All generation uses temperature $\tau{=}0.7$, nucleus sampling with $p{=}0.9$, and maximum length of 256 new tokens.
33	The theoretical yield is $8 \times {\sim}1{,}000 \times 5 \approx 40{,}000$ texts; after removing generation failures, exact duplicates, and passages shorter than 50 tokens, 37{,}058 texts remain (Appendix~\ref{app:dataset-stats}).
34	For classification, depths 2--4 are collapsed into the $2{+}$ class.
35	
36	\subsection{Feature Extraction}
37	\label{sec:features}
38	
39	The seven features are motivated by two complementary views of distributional drift.
40	Reference-model features capture how the text's token-level surprise distribution shifts relative to a fixed model; surface features capture how lexical diversity contracts under recursive generation.
41	Together, they span both the generative mechanism (what the model produces) and the surface manifestation (how the vocabulary changes); Figure~\ref{fig:framework} provides an overview.
42	This two-pronged design is not post-hoc: it follows directly from the hypothesis that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
43	
44	We extract seven distributional features per text, organized into two groups based on what they measure rather than how they are computed.
45	
46	\paragraph{Reference-model features.}
47	A held-out reference model (Pythia-410M, chosen to be smaller than all generators) computes per-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) for each text.
48	Although Pythia-410M shares the GPT-NeoX architecture with two of the eight generators, cross-family reference model experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm that depth features are not reference-specific (LOGO F1 varies by $\leq$0.013 across Pythia, OLMo, and Qwen references).
49	From the resulting NLL sequence, we extract five statistics:
50	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
51	    \item \textbf{entropy\_mean}\footnote{We use ``entropy'' as shorthand for token-level negative log-likelihood under the reference model, following convention in prior detection work. These are point-wise NLL values, not Shannon entropy of the full distribution.}: mean token-level NLL, capturing the average predictability of the text under the reference model;
52	    \item \textbf{entropy\_std}: standard deviation of token-level NLL, measuring the spread of per-token surprise;
53	    \item \textbf{entropy\_max}: maximum token-level NLL, capturing the most surprising token;
54	    \item \textbf{entropy\_min}: minimum token-level NLL, capturing the most predictable token. As generation depth increases, the floor of token-level surprise drops, reflecting the model's increasing confidence on its own outputs.
55	    Although entropy\_min shows near-zero marginal impact in leave-one-feature-out analysis ($\Delta$F1\,=\,+0.01\,pp), we retain it for completeness of the NLL summary statistics (mean, std, max, min) and because removing it does not improve performance;
56	    \item \textbf{tail\_decay}: slope of the vocabulary-level averaged log-probability distribution in the mid-rank region (ranks 100--1000).
57	    For each text, we compute the mean log-probability of each vocabulary token across all positions under the reference model, sort tokens in descending order of mean log-probability, and fit a linear regression to ranks 100--1000.
58	    The slope captures how steeply the reference model's probability mass decays beyond high-probability tokens, characterizing the shape of the distribution tail.
59	\end{itemize}
60	
61	\paragraph{Surface features.}
62	Two features capture lexical diversity without requiring a reference model:
63	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
64	    \item \textbf{TTR}: type-token ratio (number of unique word types divided by total tokens);
65	    \item \textbf{hapax\_ratio}: proportion of words appearing exactly once (\emph{hapax legomena}).
66	\end{itemize}
67	
68	\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
69	The grouping reflects an empirical pattern we term \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features (entropy\_mean, TTR, hapax\_ratio) show substantial monotonic drift with generation depth ($|\rho| = 0.60$--$0.63$); entropy\_min and entropy\_std show moderate drift ($|\rho| = 0.17$--$0.41$); and shape features (entropy\_max, tail\_decay) remain near-stationary ($|\rho| < 0.10$).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled pretraining corpora \cite{dolma,fineweb} increasingly contain LLM-generated text (estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}), and this proportion grows as generated text re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text.
Understanding how distributional features evolve across generation depths is a prerequisite for characterizing this recursive contamination, yet existing methods \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide only binary real-vs-synthetic decisions, conflating qualitatively different material: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, classifying text by generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.

The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, central-tendency and diversity features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) drift monotonically, while shape features (entropy max, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution while preserving its shape: the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constrain distributional shape under standard decoding regimes, while each successive generation compresses the location toward the model's preferred output distribution.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models as a deliberate design choice, since instruction-tuning introduces confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven shaping) that obscure this intrinsic mechanism; preliminary experiments confirm substantially degraded depth signal under instruction tuning (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves 3-class macro F1\,=\,0.809 on heterogeneous cross-model chains and F1\,=\,0.762 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation (binary F1\,=\,0.764 on cross-model chains), outperforming all individual detection baselines by 6--11\,pp while requiring only a single 410M-parameter reference model.
The signal is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show stronger drift than elaboration or rewriting (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for characterizing how distributional properties evolve across recursive generation.
    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We document differential depth response across eight generators from five families and show that a 7-feature ensemble exploiting this structure achieves competitive depth classification while requiring only a single small reference model; the interpretable feature design enables the DDR characterization in \S\ref{sec:results-differential}.
    \item \textbf{Detectable $\neq$ harmful.} Despite DDR producing measurable distributional drift, a TOST equivalence test confirms that depth-stratified text yields training utility equivalent to random subsampling ($\pm$2\% margin, $p < 0.001$) within chains of $\leq$4 generations as measured by perplexity (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}), decoupling detectability from downstream harm.
\end{enumerate}
